title: Automatic thoughts: what’s ripening in the garden of your mind?
description: This article dives into the world of automatic thoughts—the invisible companions of our emotions in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). Returning to the metaphor of an apple tree, we’ll explore how our instant reactions are born. Using a vivid real-life example, we’ll show why different life experiences cause us to interpret the same events differently, and prove that you can learn to manage this process.

texts: From the previous chapter, we’ve learned the most important thing: our thoughts are the invisible conductors of our emotions and physical reactions.
Now, building on this foundation, let’s get acquainted with the phenomenon we’ll be working with in practice every day.
To clearly illustrate how thinking works in CBT, we’ll return once more to the image of a tree.
Imagine a sprawling apple tree. It symbolizes your mind. Hanging from its branches are fruits: some are ripe and sweet, while others are bruised or rotting.
These apples on the branches are your thoughts.
In psychology, they are called “automatic.” They flash in your head instantly, like a reflex, requiring no effort at all.
They pass by so quickly and there are so many of them that we often perceive them as background noise, not even noticing how they dictate our mood.
<q author="Epictetus">It is not events that disturb us, but our opinions about them.</q>
Let’s try a little thought experiment.
Imagine this: you’re sitting in a cozy cinema seat, the lights go down, and you’re waiting for the movie to start.
Suddenly, a woman in the row in front of you stands up abruptly and sharply slaps the man sitting next to her.
The situation is shocking and tense. Try to trace what thought would flash through your mind first, and how you would feel.
Since we don’t know your personal history, it’s difficult to predict your exact reaction.
So, let’s look at the thoughts of two spectators sitting to your right and left in this scenario.
On the left sits a woman who has experienced domestic violence in the past. Here is how this scene resonates with her:

<stepper automatic="How terrifying... She’ll probably be in so much trouble when she gets home." emotions="Sadness, sticky fear, despair." behavior="Cringes in her seat, struggling to hold back tears.">
And on the right is a young man who has recently gone through a difficult, high-profile divorce:

<stepper automatic="She’s so irrational! Couldn’t she have waited until she got home instead of making a scene in front of everyone?!" emotions="Anger, sharp irritation." behavior="Clenches his fists, feels a surge of heat.">
The event is the same—a slap in a movie theater. But the emotions are polar opposites because each spectator views the scene through the unique lens of their own life experience.
These instant, lightning-fast evaluations of what is happening are exactly what we call automatic thoughts.

test.question: Automatic thoughts are...
answers: Thoughts that are impossible to change
Fleeting, numerous thoughts that arise involuntarily

texts: A logical question arises: why do we have such different automatic reactions in the exact same situation?
And does this mean that with every unpleasant event, we are doomed to fall into a spiral of negativity and depression?
Absolutely not.
Automatic thoughts hum in the background of everyone’s mind, but they don’t always turn into a psychological problem.
The secret is that these fleeting thoughts are not born in a vacuum. They are connected to our deeper internal beliefs.
Just as apples don’t hang in mid-air but draw nourishment from the branches, the trunk, and the roots, our automatic reactions are inextricably linked to our intermediate and core beliefs.
